lines.text: Your guardian angel is cheering for you!
Way to let your light shine!
Your sticker grew into a giant sticker!
You did it with no mistakes!
Play again with no mistakes to make it giant!
No mistakes next time makes it giant!
Tap each block one time as you count.
The last number you say tells how many.
Two groups snap together into one bigger group.
Two blue blocks and one yellow block.
Tap blocks to take them away.
Then count how many are left.
Sometimes you snap groups together and count them all.
Sometimes you take some away and count what's left.
A circle is round, like a ball.
A square has four sides, all the same.
And a rectangle has four sides, two long and two short.
Listen for the shape, and tap it!
An oval is like an egg.
And a diamond is like a kite.
A pizza slice is a triangle.
Look at the picture, and find its shape!
Red, blue, yellow, green, orange, and purple.
Listen for the color, and tap it!
Sorting means putting things that go together in the same basket.
Three are the same, and one is different.

lines.text: Some things are bigger and some are smaller.
Some are longer and some are shorter.
Add one lane at a time, starting with the ones.
When a lane gets ten or more, trade ten of them for one of the next lane, and it moves left.
For example, 27 plus 15: 7 plus 5 is 12 ones.
That's ten or more, so ten ones become one ten.
Take away one lane at a time, starting with the ones.
If there aren't enough, trade one from the next lane for ten, and it moves right.
Trade one ten for ten ones.
When you add and a lane gets ten or more, trade it to the left.
When you take away and a lane doesn't have enough, trade from the left, and it moves right.
For example, 258 plus 167: 8 plus 7 is 15 ones.
For example, 2476 plus 1658: 6 plus 8 is 14 ones.
Each digit's place tells what it's worth.
We say it: three hundred forty-seven.
We say it: two thousand three hundred forty-seven.

lines.text: Doubling means adding the exact same number twice, like two wings on a ladybug.

lines.text: Finding half is the opposite of doubling.

lines.text: We split an even number equally into two baskets so both baskets get the exact same amount.

lines.text: Half of 10 is 5, because 5 plus 5 makes 10!

lines.text: When two numbers are neighbors on the number line, like 5 plus 6, just double the smaller number and add 1 more!
Here you see the total, and you have to find which twin number was doubled to make it.
For 12, the twin number is 6, because 6 plus 6 equals 12!

lines.text: To double a two-digit number like 12, double the tens first, and then double the ones!

lines.text: Double 10 is 20, and double 2 is 4, which makes 24!

lines.text: When we skip-count, we add the same number on every hop.
Find the number that belongs on the orange stone.

lines.text: Multiplication is a fast way to add equal groups.
lines.where: How it works: Equal Groups (Groups of Beads)

lines.text: The multiplication sign means groups of.
lines.where: How it works: Equal Groups (Groups of Beads)

lines.text: So 3 times 4 means 3 groups of 4, which is 4 plus 4 plus 4 equals 12!

lines.where: How it works: Array Rows × Columns

lines.text: Multiplying by 2 is just doubling once.
To solve 4 times 6, double 6 to get 12, then double 12 to get 24!

lines.text: Multiplying by 10 is easy with Golden Ten-Bars: 10 times 6 is 6 tens, which is 60.

lines.text: And since 5 is half of 10, 5 times 6 is half of 60, which is 30!

lines.text: Division means sharing a total equally.

lines.text: When a multiplication equation has a missing number, like 4 times blank equals 20, count by 4s until you reach 20: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 — that is 5 fours!

lines.text: Every part is the same size.
This pizza is cut into four fair shares.
This one isn't fair: some pieces are big and some are small.
Sharing fairly is a way to love our neighbor!
When we cut something into two equal parts, each part is one half.
When we cut it into four equal parts, each part is one fourth.
Like the four candles of the Advent wreath: light one, and one fourth are lit!
Tap a part to shade it.
Two thirds means two of the three equal parts.
Tap the parts to shade them, then press check.
The top number counts the shaded parts.
The bottom number counts all the equal parts.
Three parts are shaded, out of four equal parts.
The space from zero to one is cut into equal jumps.
For two fourths, the bottom number says four jumps in all.
Different fractions can be the same amount.
One half and two fourths cover the same part of the bar, so they are equal.
Like sharing loaves of bread: more, smaller pieces can be the same amount of bread.
When the bottom numbers are the same, more parts is bigger.
When the top numbers are the same, more cuts make smaller pieces.
So one eighth is less than one half.

Tap the drum once for each beat, then press done.

The letter i says {{ih}}, like insect, and pig.
Let's sound out words with {{ih}} in the middle!
The letter o says {{aw}}, like octopus, and dog.

Tap each letter to hear its sound.
Now slide them together, faster and faster: {{kuh}} {{ah}} {{tuh}}, cat!

The letter e says {{eh}}, like egg, and bed.

I, n, g says {{ing}}: jump, jumping!

lines.text: Some word endings have their very own sound.
T, i, o, n says {{shun}}, like station.
T, u, r, e says {{cher}}, like picture.
And l, e at the end says {{ul}}, like candle, and turtle.
These endings change a word's meaning.
F, u, l means full of: playful, thankful.
L, e, s, s means without: fearless.
N, e, s, s turns a word into a thing: kind, kindness.
Every kind of word has its own shape and color.
Article: a small light blue triangle.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a punctuation mark.
Tap or drag the words in order so the sentence makes sense!
The very first word of every sentence must begin with a big capital letter.
Look at all the words in the sentence and tap the word that needs a capital start!
Words need a comfy space between them so we can read them clearly.
Find the two words that got squished together and tap right between the letters where they should split!
Every sentence ends with a mark in the orange box.
Use a period for a telling sentence, a question mark when asking a question, and an exclamation mark for big excitement!
Names of people and pets, and the word I by itself, are special!
They always start with a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence.
A noun is a naming word for a person, place, animal, or thing.
We mark every noun with a big black triangle.
In the example below, puppy is a noun because a puppy is an animal!
A verb is an action word that tells what someone or something does, like run, jump, or sing.
We mark verbs with a bright red circle.
In this example, jumped is the action verb!
An adjective is a describing word that tells what kind, what color, or how many, like fluffy, red, or two.
We mark adjectives with a medium blue triangle.
Most words add S to mean more than one, like dogs.
Words ending in S, X, Z, CH, or SH add E-S, like boxes or foxes.
Pick the right plural word to fill the orange space!
Say an before a word that starts with a vowel sound, like an apple, or an owl.

lines.text: Proper nouns are special names for days of the week, months, holidays, cities, and people.
Tap every proper noun to give it a capital letter!
Commas help readers pause in the right spot!

lines.text: A contraction squishes two words together and uses an apostrophe to show where letters were left out!
For example, do not becomes don't, and I am becomes I'm.
A pro-noun is a little word that takes the place of a noun or name, like she, he, they, we, I, or you.
We mark pro-nouns with a tall purple triangle.
In this example, She takes the place of a person's name!
An adverb describes an action verb and tells how, when, or where something happened.
Many adverbs end in L-Y, like quickly, softly, or loudly.
We mark adverbs with a small orange circle!
Past tense verbs tell about actions that already happened yesterday or before!
lines.where: How it works: ⏳ Past Tense Verbs

lines.text: Many verbs add E-D like climbed, while special verbs change spelling, like eat becomes ate and go becomes went!
lines.where: How it works: ⏳ Past Tense Verbs

lines.text: Some plural nouns are tricky and change their spelling instead of adding S!
One mouse becomes two mice, one child becomes many children, and one sheep stays sheep!
A complete sentence must have two parts: a subject that tells who or what, and a verb that tells what happened!

lines.text: Quotation marks hug the exact words a person says out loud!
Put quotation marks at the beginning and end of what was spoken, with the punctuation mark tucked inside.
Possessive nouns show who owns something!
Add apostrophe S for one owner, like the cat's collar.
Put the apostrophe after the S for more than one owner, like the puppies' tails!
A preposition is a bridge word that shows where or when, like in, on, under, over, or into.
We mark prepositions with a green crescent bridge.
Here, under shows where the puppy hid!
A conjunction is a linking word that joins words or ideas together, like and, but, or, so, and because.
We mark conjunctions with a pink bar!
When the subject is just one person or animal, the present-tense action verb adds an S, like The puppy eats.
When the subject is more than one, the verb does not add S, like The kittens dance!
When we compare two things, we add E-R or use more, like faster than.
When we compare three or more things, we add E-S-T or use most, like the highest mountain!
